title: CHEM1A Practice Quiz — Objective 4: Reactions, Aqueous Chemistry & Stoichiometry (DRAFT pending Gilley approval)

items.stem: When ___Fe + ___Cl₂ → ___FeCl₃ is balanced with the smallest whole-number coefficients, the coefficient of Cl₂ is:
items.explain: 2 Fe + 3 Cl₂ → 2 FeCl₃ (Fe 2/2, Cl 6/6). Choosing 2 reads iron's coefficient as chlorine's; 1 leaves chlorine unbalanced; 6 balances atoms but is not the smallest set (it doubles everything).

items.stem: Which equation is correctly balanced?
items.explain: C 2/2, H 4/4, O 6 = 4 + 2. The second is unbalanced; the third changed a SUBSCRIPT (H₂O to H₂O₂ — a different substance); the fourth has only 4 oxygens on the left for 6 on the right.

items.stem: The reaction 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂ is best classified as:
items.explain: One substance breaks into two — decomposition. Synthesis is the reverse pattern; nothing displaces anything; there is no fuel + O₂ reactant pattern (oxygen is a PRODUCT here).

items.stem: Which reaction is a double displacement?
items.explain: Two compounds swap partners (Ba/Na trade anions), and the swap strands barium with sulfate as insoluble BaSO₄ — a precipitation predicted straight from the solubility rules. Zn + HCl is single displacement (an element displaces H); H₂ + Cl₂ is synthesis; CH₄ + O₂ is combustion.

items.stem: Which reaction is a synthesis (combination) reaction?
items.explain: Two substances combine into one — the synthesis pattern (A + B → AB). 2 HgO → 2 Hg + O₂ is decomposition (one substance becomes two); Fe + CuSO₄ is single displacement (iron displaces copper); K₂CO₃ + MgCl₂ is double displacement (partner swap).

items.stem: Which 0.1 M solution conducts electricity best?
choices: They all conduct equally at equal concentration
items.explain: NaCl dissociates completely — a strong electrolyte, maximum ions per formula unit dissolved. Sugar dissolves without forming ions (nonelectrolyte); acetic acid only partially ionizes (weak electrolyte). Conduction depends on IONS, not on how much dissolved.

items.stem: Nitrous acid (HNO₂) is a weak acid. In aqueous solution it exists mostly as:
choices: Intact HNO₂ molecules, with a small fraction ionized to H⁺ and NO₂⁻
Completely separated H⁺ and NO₂⁻ ions
items.explain: Weak electrolyte = partial ionization — most molecules stay whole. Complete dissociation describes a STRONG acid; the other options confuse dissolving with reacting.

items.stem: Mixing which pair of aqueous solutions produces a precipitate?
items.explain: The swap gives BaSO₄ — the classic sulfate exception (Ba²⁺/Pb²⁺/Ca²⁺/Sr²⁺). NaCl + KNO₃ and NaNO₃ + K₂CO₃ give only soluble products (group 1 and nitrates are always soluble); HCl + KOH neutralizes to water — no solid.

items.stem: According to the solubility rules, which compound IS soluble in water?
items.explain: Ammonium compounds are ALWAYS soluble — that rule outranks the carbonate rule. CaCO₃ (carbonate), Fe(OH)₃ (hydroxide), and AgBr (silver halide) are all standard insolubles.

items.stem: For AgNO₃(aq) + KBr(aq) → AgBr(s) + KNO₃(aq), the spectator ions are:
choices: There are no spectator ions in a precipitation reaction
items.explain: K⁺ and NO₃⁻ appear unchanged on both sides and cancel. Ag⁺ and Br⁻ are the ions that actually react (they form the solid) — the net ionic equation is Ag⁺ + Br⁻ → AgBr(s).

items.stem: When writing a complete ionic equation, which species is NOT split into ions?
items.explain: Solids, liquids, gases, and weak electrolytes stay whole — only dissolved strong electrolytes dissociate. NaCl(aq) and KNO₃(aq) are soluble ionic compounds and HCl is a strong acid: all three split.

items.stem: Which compound is an Arrhenius base?
items.explain: KOH raises the OH⁻ concentration in water — the Arrhenius base definition. HBr is an acid (raises H⁺); CH₄ and NaCl do neither.

items.stem: When aqueous sodium carbonate reacts with excess hydrochloric acid, the gas produced is:
items.explain: Carbonates + acid → salt + water + CO₂ (carbonic acid forms first, then splits). H₂ comes from metals + acid, not carbonates; O₂ and Cl₂ come from neither.

items.stem: A solution has [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ M. Its pH is:
items.explain: pH = −log(10⁻⁸) = 8.00, above 7 = basic. High pH means LOW [H⁺] — the scale runs backwards from instinct; the sign options drop the negative in the definition.

items.stem: The pH of a solution drops from 6.00 to 3.00. The H⁺ concentration has:
items.explain: Each pH unit is a factor of ten: three units = 10³ = 1000, and DOWN in pH means UP in acidity. 'Factor of 3' reads the log scale as linear; 'decreased' inverts the scale's direction.

items.stem: What is the oxidation number of Cl in KClO₄?
items.explain: K is +1, each O is −2: 1 + x − 8 = 0 → x = +7. −1 is chlorine's number in simple chlorides (pattern-matched from memory); +4 miscounts the oxygens; +1 is potassium's number.

items.stem: What is the oxidation number of C in CO₃²⁻?
items.explain: x + 3(−2) = −2 → x = +4. −4 flips the algebra sign; +6 forgets the ion's −2 charge (treats it as neutral); 0 confuses 'element in a compound' with 'element in its natural form.'

items.stem: In Zn + 2 HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂, the species that is REDUCED is:
choices: H⁺ — its oxidation number falls from +1 to 0
Nothing is reduced; this is an acid-base reaction
items.explain: Reduction = oxidation number decreasing: H goes +1 → 0. Zn goes 0 → +2 (oxidized — dissolving is not the criterion); Cl⁻ stays −1 throughout (spectator); a reaction with oxidation-number changes IS redox.

items.stem: A substance whose oxidation number DECREASES during a reaction is:
choices: Reduced — and it is the oxidizing agent
Reduced — and it is the reducing agent
Oxidized — and it is the oxidizing agent
Oxidized — and it is the reducing agent
items.explain: Number down = gained electrons = reduced; the thing being reduced is what CAUSES the other's oxidation, so it is the oxidizing agent. The crossover naming is the whole trap — the agent is named for what it does to the OTHER substance.

items.stem: When balancing a half-reaction in acidic solution, oxygen atoms are balanced by adding:
items.explain: The acidic-solution order: atoms first, then O with H₂O, then H with H⁺, then charge with electrons. OH⁻ belongs to the BASIC-solution finish; O₂ and electrons never balance oxygen.

items.stem: The correctly balanced half-reaction for Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ is:
items.explain: Charge check: left +2, right +3 − 1 = +2 ✓ — the lost electron is a PRODUCT of oxidation. Adding the electron to the left describes reduction; two electrons overshoots the one-unit change; no oxygen means no H₂O is involved.

items.stem: For 2 CO + O₂ → 2 CO₂, how many grams of CO₂ (44.01 g/mol) form from 0.400 mol of CO with excess oxygen?
items.explain: 0.400 mol CO × (2 CO₂/2 CO) = 0.400 mol × 44.01 g/mol = 17.6 g. 35.2 doubles the ratio (misreads 2:2 as 1:2); 8.80 halves it; 0.400 reports moles as grams.

items.stem: In a mass-to-mass calculation, the balanced equation enters at exactly one step — which?
choices: The mole-ratio step between the given and wanted substances
The grams-to-moles conversion of the given substance
The moles-to-grams conversion of the wanted substance
The significant-figures decision at the end
items.explain: The coefficients supply the exchange rate between substances; both molar-mass steps use only the periodic table. Knowing WHERE the equation matters is what makes the chain transferable to any reaction.

items.stem: 5.0 mol of CO and 3.0 mol of O₂ react: 2 CO + O₂ → 2 CO₂. The limiting reactant is:
choices: CO — dividing by coefficients gives CO: 2.5 and O₂: 3.0
O₂ — there are fewer moles of it
CO₂ — it is produced in the smallest amount
items.explain: Divide by coefficient: CO 5.0/2 = 2.5, O₂ 3.0/1 = 3.0 — the smaller result limits. 'Fewer moles' ignores the 2:1 stoichiometry (the classic trap); a PRODUCT can never be limiting.

items.stem: 2.0 mol of SO₂ and 1.5 mol of O₂ react completely: 2 SO₂ + O₂ → 2 SO₃. How many moles of the excess reactant remain?
items.explain: SO₂: 2.0/2 = 1.0; O₂: 1.5/1 = 1.5 → SO₂ limits. O₂ used = 2.0 mol SO₂ × (1 O₂/2 SO₂) = 1.0 mol; remaining = 1.5 − 1.0 = 0.5 mol. 1.5 forgets any O₂ reacted; the SO₂ option picks the wrong reactant as excess.

items.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 15.5 g. The experiment collects 12.4 g. The percent yield is:
items.explain: 12.4/15.5 × 100 = 80.0% — actual over theoretical. 125% inverts the fraction (a percent yield above 100 from a division flip); 3.1 subtracts; 12.4 reports the actual mass as a percent.

items.stem: A synthesis runs at 65.0 percent yield. To actually collect 13.0 g of product, the theoretical yield you must aim for is:
items.explain: Theoretical = actual ÷ yield = 13.0/0.650 = 20.0 g — you scale UP, because the actual is only a fraction of the theoretical. 8.45 multiplies instead of divides (scales the wrong way); the reverse-yield direction is a known final-exam demand.

items.stem: How many moles of NaOH are in 50.0 mL of a 0.200 M solution?
items.explain: M × V = 0.200 mol/L × 0.0500 L = 0.0100 mol. 10.0 forgets the mL→L conversion; 0.250 divides M by V; 4.00 divides V by M. The M × V door is how moles enter every solution-stoichiometry chain.

items.stem: A 30.00 mL sample of HCl is neutralized by 15.00 mL of 0.400 M NaOH (1:1 ratio). The molarity of the HCl is:
items.explain: Moles NaOH = 0.01500 × 0.400 = 0.00600 mol = moles HCl; 0.00600/0.03000 L = 0.200 M. 0.133 divides by the COMBINED volume (45.00 mL) — the acid's moles live in the acid's volume alone; 0.400 assumes equal volumes mean equal molarity; 0.00600 reports moles as molarity.

items.stem: In a gravimetric analysis, the mass that is actually weighed is:
choices: The dried, insoluble precipitate that carries the ion being measured
The water evaporated from the solution
items.explain: The analyte ion is captured quantitatively in an insoluble solid, dried, and weighed — the precipitate's mass walks back through moles to the ion's concentration. The other options measure nothing about the analyte.

items.stem: Excess BaCl₂ precipitates all the sulfate from a 100.0 mL sample as BaSO₄ (233.40 g/mol). The dried solid weighs 0.467 g. The sulfate-ion molarity of the sample was:
items.explain: 0.467/233.40 = 0.00200 mol BaSO₄ = 0.00200 mol SO₄²⁻; ÷ 0.1000 L = 0.0200 M. 0.00200 reports moles as molarity (skips the volume); 0.200 slips the mL→L conversion; 4.67 divides grams by volume.

items.stem: The theoretical yield of a reaction is:
choices: The maximum amount of product the limiting reactant could form, computed from stoichiometry
The amount of product actually collected in the laboratory
The percent of reactant converted to product
The amount of excess reactant remaining
items.explain: Theoretical = the stoichiometric maximum (calculated, not measured). The actual yield is what the bench delivers; percent yield compares the two; leftover excess is a different bookkeeping line entirely.

items.stem: A net ionic equation shows:
choices: Only the species that actually change during the reaction, with spectators removed
Every ion present in the mixed solutions
The same information as the molecular equation, in different notation
items.explain: Net ionic = complete ionic minus the spectators — the chemistry that actually happened. 'Every ion' describes the COMPLETE ionic equation; solids alone omit the reacting ions; the molecular equation hides which species are dissociated.
